verdict.summary:
REGULATORY ANSWER — MINIMUM REST BETWEEN DUTY DAYS FOR A US AIRLINE FLIGHT ATTENDANT

=== 1. BOTTOM LINE ===

A US airline operating under 14 CFR Part 121 must give a flight attendant a scheduled rest period of at least 10 CONSECUTIVE HOURS between the completion of one scheduled duty period and the commencement of the next. That is the federal floor, set by 14 CFR § 121.467 ("Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements: Domestic, flag, and supplemental operations").

There is exactly one way the number drops below 10: the reduced-rest provision, which permits 8 consecutive hours only if the carrier then gives a subsequent (compensatory) rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest. 8 hours is never a free-standing minimum; it is a loan that must be repaid within the same 24-hour window.

So: 10 hours is the answer; 8 hours is the conditional exception; anything above 10 comes from a collective bargaining agreement or company policy, not from the regulation.

=== 2. REGULATORY BASIS AND SCOPE ===

Citation: 14 CFR § 121.467, titled "Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements: Domestic, flag, and supplemental operations." The section sits in Part 121, Subpart P (Flight Attendants), and by its own terms applies to domestic, flag, and supplemental operations alike.

Consequence for the question as posed: the type-of-operation ambiguity does not change the headline number. The research base specifically found no separate rest figure that varies by the domestic/flag/supplemental label; the operative variables inside § 121.467 are (a) the length of the scheduled duty period and (b) whether the carrier is using the reduced-rest option. Do not tell an operator that "flag gets 12 and domestic gets 10" — that is not what this section does.

Scope limits worth stating in the answer:
- This is the FAA minimum. It is a floor, not a ceiling. CBAs routinely exceed it.
- It is a Part 121 scheduled-passenger rule. Part 135 on-demand/commuter operations are not covered by § 121.467 and have no equivalent flight-attendant rest minimum.
- It is a scheduling rule: the carrier must schedule the rest, and the rest must actually fall between the two duty periods.

=== 3. THE RULE, AS VERIFIED ===

Verified text (eCFR, § 121.467):

- Duty period of 14 hours or less — "(2) A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

- Reduced rest — "(3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

Summary table (federal minimum, § 121.467):

| Situation | Scheduled rest required | Condition / repayment |
|---|---|---|
| Duty period of 14 h or less (the normal case) | 10 consecutive hours | None — this is the baseline |
| Same, using reduced rest | 8 consecutive hours | Subsequent rest of >= 10 consecutive hours, scheduled to begin no later than 24 h after the start of the reduced rest, and itself falling between the two duty periods |
| Duty period over 14 h (extended under the section) | 12 consecutive hours (PROVISIONAL — see § 5) | Reducible to 10 consecutive hours only with a subsequent rest of >= 14 consecutive hours |

=== 4. WHAT COUNTS AS REST, AND HOW IT IS MEASURED ===

- Consecutive clock hours, not "hours off minus commute." The clock runs from completion of the scheduled duty period to commencement of the subsequent duty period. Hotel transport and post-flight duties that occur inside the duty period do not eat the rest; anything the carrier requires after the duty period ends does.
- Free from duty. The flight attendant must be relieved of all duty. Airport standby, hotel standby, being on call, and required training are duty, not rest.
- Between duty periods. This is the overnight/inter-duty rest figure. It is not the same as an intra-duty-day break between flight segments, and it is not a weekly rest day. If the questioner meant a break inside a single duty day, the answer is "the regulation sets no separate intra-duty-day break minimum; that comes from the CBA or company policy" — do not answer that with 10 hours.
- The rule is written in terms of the SCHEDULED rest period. Operationally, carriers must still deliver it: if actual block-in and actual report compress the gap below the scheduled minimum, the carrier is out of compliance for that pairing and must restore the rest before the next assignment. Build the check on actual times, not just the printed schedule.

=== 5. DUTY PERIODS LONGER THAN 14 HOURS (PROVISIONAL — VERIFY BEFORE RELYING) ===

The research base reports a second tier: for a duty period of more than 14 hours but not more than 20 hours, a scheduled rest of at least 12 consecutive hours, reducible to 10 consecutive hours only if a subsequent rest of at least 14 consecutive hours is provided. No quoted eCFR passage was retrieved for that tier, so it is carried here as provisional.

What that means practically: the tier does not change the answer to the question asked. Every figure in it (12, and the reduced 10) is at or above the 10-hour baseline, so it cannot conflict with the headline value. If the answer is being relied on for a specific pairing that pushes past a 14-hour scheduled duty period, pull the current eCFR text of § 121.467(b) and confirm the paragraph numbering and figures before signing off. Treat the 12-hour tier as unconfirmed until then.

=== 6. WORKED COMPLIANCE EXAMPLES ===

Example A — standard rest.
Duty period 1 ends (block-in plus post-flight duties complete) at 20:00 local, Day 1. Earliest permissible report for duty period 2 is 06:00 local, Day 2 (20:00 + 10 h). Compliant.

Example B — reduced rest.
Same 20:00 release. Carrier elects reduced rest: earliest report is 04:00, Day 2 (20:00 + 8 h). To use this, the carrier must schedule a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 20:00, Day 2 (24 hours after the reduced rest began at 20:00, Day 1). That means the flight attendant must be released from duty period 2 no later than 20:00, Day 2, and remain off duty until at least 06:00, Day 3. Compliant only if both legs of the repayment are scheduled.

Example C — non-compliant.
Release 20:00, Day 1; report 04:00, Day 2 (8 h, reduced rest used); duty period 2 released 23:00, Day 2. The compensatory rest cannot begin by 20:00, Day 2 because the flight attendant is still on duty. Violation of § 121.467(b)(3).

=== 7. INTERPLAY WITH OTHER LIMITS ===

- Duty period limits are the other half of the rule. Rest and duty period length are a matched pair in § 121.467: the rest figure is keyed to the scheduled duty period, so a carrier cannot stretch duty and keep the 10-hour rest. Check duty period limits in the same section whenever the pairing is near 14 hours.
- Deadheading: a flight attendant deadheading is on duty, so deadhead time counts against the duty period and cannot be counted as rest.
- Reserve/standby: airport standby and short-call reserve are duty. Rest starts only when the flight attendant is actually relieved.
- Training: required training is duty.
- Weekly/24-in-7 rest is a separate requirement and does not satisfy the between-duty-days rest obligation.
- State law: airline service is broadly federally preempted (49 U.S.C. § 41713), so a state rest rule will not normally set the between-duty-days figure for a Part 121 carrier. State wage-and-hour law can still affect pay for the rest period. Do not offer a state rule as the answer to this question.

=== 8. WHAT SITS ABOVE THE MINIMUM ===

10 hours is the FAA floor. Collective bargaining agreements and company policies commonly require more, and it is routine for agreements to specify a longer overnight rest, and longer still on international/flag sequences. If the questioner is asking what THEIR airline must give, the answer is: the greater of § 121.467 and the applicable CBA or company manual. The regulatory answer above is the floor from which that comparison starts.

=== 9. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST (for anyone relying on this) ===

1. Pull the current text of 14 CFR § 121.467 from eCFR (Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter G, Part 121, Subpart P). Confirm the paragraph (b) structure and that 10 h / 8 h reduced are unchanged as of the date of reliance.
2. Confirm the operation type is Part 121 domestic, flag, or supplemental — all three are covered by this section.
3. Confirm whether the pairing in question exceeds a 14-hour scheduled duty period; if so, resolve the provisional 12-hour tier in § 5 against the eCFR text.
4. Pull the applicable CBA rest article and the company manual; take the greater figure.
5. Check actual (not just scheduled) release and report times for the specific pairing.
6. Check for any applicable exemption, waiver, or SFAR covering the carrier or the operation.

=== 10. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID ===

- Reporting 8 hours as "the" minimum. It is the reduced-rest exception and carries a same-window 10-hour repayment.
- Reporting a single number that varies by domestic vs. flag. § 121.467 covers all three operation types; the variable is duty period length, not the operation label.
- Confusing this with a weekly rest day or an intra-duty-day break.
- Quoting a CBA figure as if it were the regulation, or the regulation as if it were the CBA entitlement.

=== 11. ASSUMPTIONS ===

Current federal law as reflected in the current eCFR; Part 121 scheduled passenger carrier; a working (not deadheading, not on reserve) flight attendant; the question means the overnight rest between duty periods, not a break inside a duty day. If the questioner meant a break inside a single duty day, or a non-Part-121 operator, the answer changes and this analysis does not apply.

verdict.summary:
# Maximum weight for a drone to count as a 'small unmanned aircraft' under FAA rules

## Bottom line

**Less than 55 pounds (lb) on takeoff — 24.9476 kg — including everything on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.**

55 lb is the threshold, and it is **exclusive**: an aircraft that weighs exactly 55.000 lb on takeoff does **not** qualify. The qualifying maximum is therefore any takeoff weight strictly below 55 lb. In practice, plan to a working limit of **54.9 lb / 24.90 kg** to stay clear of the boundary and of scale tolerance.

## Controlling rule text

14 CFR 107.3 (definitions), Part 107 — Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems:

> *Small unmanned aircraft* means an unmanned aircraft weighing **less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft**.

The same 'less than 55 pounds' definition of 'small unmanned aircraft' is carried in the statute for the recreational/educational exception (49 U.S.C. § 44809, incorporating the § 44801 definition), so the 55 lb line is the same for both the Part 107 path and the recreational exception path. The definition is not rule-set-dependent in the way the threshold for *operations over people* is; it is the single gate that determines whether an aircraft is a small UAS at all.

## What counts toward the 55 lb

The rule is explicit and leaves no discretion: **'including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft.'**

That means the weighed figure is a takeoff (all-up) weight, and it includes at minimum:

- airframe and structure
- propulsion batteries / fuel
- cameras, gimbals, sensors, LiDAR, lights, speakers, spray tanks and their contents
- attached antennas, strobes, parachutes, tether hardware, cargo-release mechanisms, mounts, brackets and fasteners
- any payload carried for the mission

It does **not** help to characterise an item as 'payload' or 'removable': if it is on board or attached at takeoff, it counts. A drone whose empty weight is under 55 lb can still be a non-small UAS once mission equipment is fitted. Conversely, you cannot 'create' a small UAS by removing equipment after takeoff — the weight is assessed on takeoff (Category 1 operations additionally require the weight to hold *throughout* the operation, but the 55 lb classification test is a takeoff test).

## Unit conversions and the boundary (do not round across the line)

| Figure | Value | Qualifies as small UAS? |
|---|---|---|
| Rule threshold | 55 lb | No — 'less than 55' is exclusive |
| Metric equivalent of threshold | 24.9476 kg | No — identical to 55 lb |
| Recommended working limit | 54.9 lb = 24.90 kg | Yes |
| Common metric round number | 25 kg = 55.1156 lb | **No** — exceeds 55 lb |

Two traps worth calling out explicitly because they recur in real programmes:

1. **25 kg is not the US limit.** 25 kg (55.12 lb) is the open-category limit in the EU and the limit in Canada; it is *over* the FAA line. A vehicle designed to '25 kg' is not a small UAS in the US.
2. **No published rounding tolerance.** The FAA has not published a grace band around 55 lb. Treat 54.99 lb as the arithmetic ceiling and 54.9 lb as the engineering ceiling.

## Thresholds that are routinely confused with the 55 lb line

These are separate tests; none of them changes the 55 lb classification limit.

| Threshold | What it governs | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **< 55 lb** | Whether the aircraft is a 'small unmanned aircraft' at all | 14 CFR 107.3 |
| **≤ 0.55 lb (≈249.5 g)** | Category 1 operations over people / moving vehicles; must hold on takeoff **and throughout** the operation, same 'everything on board or attached' convention | 14 CFR 107 Subpart D, § 107.110(a)(1) |
| **< 55 lb** | Category 2 and Category 3 operations over people (Category 2 also requires no exposed rotating parts that would lacerate skin) | 14 CFR 107 Subpart D |
| **~0.55 lb / 250 g** | Separate *registration* trigger for recreational flyers under Part 48 (Part 107 operations carry their own registration obligation independent of weight) | 14 CFR Part 48 |

Note on the 0.55 lb / 250 g pair: 0.55 lb = 249.48 g, and 250 g = 0.5512 lb. They are close but not equal. If a design is being held to Category 1, hold it to **0.55 lb**, not to 250 g.

## What happens above 55 lb

An unmanned aircraft of 55 lb or more on takeoff is **not a small unmanned aircraft**, and therefore:

- Part 107 does not apply to it, and a Part 107 waiver cannot fix this — the waiver provisions operate on the operating rules for *small* UAS, not on the definition itself. There is no Part 107 mechanism that authorises operating a non-small UAS.
- It must be flown under a different authority — typically an airworthiness certificate (e.g. Part 21) for a certificated UAS, or an exemption (e.g. under 49 U.S.C. § 44807) with the associated conditions and limitations, or another applicable operating rule (e.g. agricultural operations under Part 137 with the relevant exemption).
- It may also fall outside the recreational exception, which is limited to small unmanned aircraft.

## Practitioner verification procedure

1. Identify the heaviest configuration that will be flown, not the lightest.
2. Weigh the aircraft **as it will be at takeoff** — batteries installed, payload loaded, all attachments fitted, spray/cargo tanks at full.
3. Use a calibrated scale; record the reading and the configuration.
4. Confirm the reading is **strictly below 55.0 lb**. If the reading is 54.9 lb or above, re-weigh on a second scale and consider reducing configuration, because you are inside scale and configuration-variance range.
5. Separately check the operating category: if the mission involves flight over people or moving vehicles, the applicable limit is 0.55 lb (Category 1), ≤55 lb with no lacerating exposed rotating parts (Category 2), or ≤55 lb with the Category 3 operating restrictions — not the bare 55 lb classification limit.
6. Separately check registration obligations under Part 48 and the Part 107 registration requirement.
7. Record the takeoff weight in the operating documentation so the classification basis is auditable.

## Scope note

This answer is the US FAA position under 14 CFR Part 107 (and the parallel statutory definition used by the recreational exception), current as of the rule text retrieved for this analysis. If the operation is under a non-US authority, the number is different — the EU open category and Canada both use 25 kg, and the UK uses 20 kg — and this answer does not apply to those jurisdictions.

## Sources

- 14 CFR 107.3, definitions — eCFR, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 107, Subpart A: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-F/part-107/subpart-A/section-107.3
- 14 CFR Part 107, Subpart D (Category 1 weight requirement, § 107.110(a)(1)) — GovInfo, CFR-2026-title14-vol2: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol2/xml/CFR-2026-title14-vol2-part107.xml
- 14 CFR Part 48 (registration): https://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-48
- FAA, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (Part 107) rule page: https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/small-unmanned-aircraft-systems-uas-regulations-part-107
- FAA AC 107-2, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems: https://www.faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/advisory_circular/ac_107-2.pdf

# Basic VFR Weather Minimums — Class E Airspace Below 10,000 ft MSL

**Governing standard:** 14 CFR § 91.155, "Basic VFR weather minimums" (United States, FAA). Restated in the AIM (Airspace chapter, VFR cruising/weather minimums table).

## 1. The answer

For Class E airspace **below 10,000 ft MSL**:

| Element | Minimum |
|---|---|
| Flight visibility | **3 statute miles** |
| Distance from clouds — below | **500 ft** |
| Distance from clouds — above | **1,000 ft** |
| Distance from clouds — horizontal | **2,000 ft** |

Mnemonic: *3 miles, 5-1-2* (500 below / 1,000 above / 2,000 horizontal).

**Verbatim table row (eCFR, § 91.155):**

```
|Airspace|Flight visibility|Distance from clouds|
|Class E:| | |
|Less than 10,000 feet MSL|3 statute miles|500 feet below.|
| | |1,000 feet above.|
| | |2,000 feet horizontal.|
```

## 2. Boundary condition at 10,000 ft MSL

The rule is written as two rows with a hard split at 10,000 ft MSL. The adjacent row reads **"Class E: At or above 10,000 feet MSL — 5 statute miles; 1,000 ft below; 1,000 ft above; 1 statute mile horizontal."** Therefore:

- The 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 figures apply **strictly below** 10,000 ft MSL.
- **At exactly 10,000 ft MSL** the higher row applies (5 SM; 1,000 below; 1,000 above; 1 SM horizontal). An aircraft cruising at 10,000 ft MSL in Class E is on the 5 SM standard, not the 3 SM standard.
- Altitudes are **MSL**, not AGL, for this split. (The 10,000 ft MSL row is an MSL test; do not substitute AGL.)

## 3. Scope notes and common misreadings

1. **No day/night difference in Class E.** The same 3 SM / 500-1,000-2,000 applies day and night. The day/night tightening that pilots associate with "1 SM clear of clouds" belongs to **Class G**, not Class E.
2. **Both flavors of Class E use the same numbers.** Class E surface areas (sfc–upward, e.g. airport surface areas) and Class E that begins at 700 ft or 1,200 ft AGL both fall under this row when below 10,000 ft MSL. Surface-area designation adds ceiling and ground-visibility provisions (§ 91.155(b), (c)) but does **not** change the visibility/cloud-clearance figures.
3. **Units matter.** Visibility is in **statute miles** (not nautical miles); cloud clearance is in **feet**. 3 SM ≈ 2.6 NM — do not report it as 3 NM.
4. **Jurisdiction.** These figures are FAA-specific. A non-FAA authority (e.g. EASA/SERA, or a national AIP) uses different numeric minima for Class E. If the operation is not under 14 CFR, this answer does not apply and the applicable authority's VMC table must be consulted.

## 4. Provisions deliberately excluded from the "basic" answer (flag, do not apply)

These modify the basic figures in specific circumstances; none of them changes the § 91.155(a) table answer above.

- **§ 91.155(b) — ceiling.** Within the lateral boundaries of the surface areas of Class B, C, D, or E airspace designated for an airport, VFR flight beneath a ceiling of less than 1,000 ft is prohibited (except under Special VFR).
- **§ 91.155(c) — ground visibility.** At those same airports: at least 3 SM **ground** visibility to take off, land, or enter the traffic pattern; if ground visibility is not reported, flight visibility during landing/takeoff or in the pattern must be at least 3 SM.
- **§ 91.157 — Special VFR.** Requires ATC authorization; minimum is **1 SM flight visibility and clear of clouds**, at or below 10,000 ft MSL, with additional pilot/equipment/currency conditions at night. This is a clearance-based exception, not a basic minimum.
- **§ 91.155(d) — helicopters.** Helicopters may operate with 1/2 SM flight visibility if outside Class B/C/D/E surface areas and at a speed permitting adequate see-and-avoid.
- **Class G rows** of the same table (1 SM clear of clouds at/below 1,200 ft AGL by day, etc.) — different airspace class, not responsive to this ask.

## 5. How to apply (checklist for a flight-planning or dispatch use)

1. Confirm the airspace is Class E at the planned altitude (not B, C, D, or G).
2. Confirm planned altitude is **below** 10,000 ft MSL; if at or above, switch to 5 SM / 1,000 below / 1,000 above / 1 SM horizontal.
3. Check forecast/actual flight visibility against **3 SM**.
4. Check cloud clearance against **500 ft below / 1,000 ft above / 2,000 ft horizontal**.
5. If operating to/from an airport inside a Class E surface area, additionally verify ceiling ≥ 1,000 ft and 3 SM ground visibility (§ 91.155(b), (c)).

**Source:** 14 CFR § 91.155 table, as published on eCFR (fetched 2026-11-15, sha256 0c42be574c1f), corroborated by FAA AIM guidance on VFR weather minimums.

verdict.summary:
OSHA limits for respirable crystalline silica — general industry

Governing standard: 29 CFR 1910.1053, "Respirable Crystalline Silica" (general industry and maritime). Construction and shipyard work are governed by separate rules (29 CFR 1926.1153 for construction); the numbers happen to be identical, but the compliance obligations are not, so citing the construction rule for general-industry work is a standards-selection error.

1. Permissible exposure limit (PEL)
- Value: 50 µg/m³ (0.05 mg/m³) of respirable crystalline silica, calculated as an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA).
- Citation: 29 CFR 1910.1053(c).
- Meaning: the employer must ensure no employee is exposed above this level, as an 8-hour TWA, on any shift. Exceeding the PEL triggers the methods-of-compliance duty (engineering controls where feasible), regulated-area requirements, and respiratory-protection obligations.

2. Action level (AL)
- Value: 25 µg/m³ (0.025 mg/m³) of respirable crystalline silica, calculated as an 8-hour TWA.
- Citation: 29 CFR 1910.1053(b) (definition of "action level").
- Relationship: the AL is defined independently in the standard, not as a formula, and is numerically one-half of the PEL. Both are 8-hour TWA concentrations of the respirable fraction.

Quick-reference table
| Quantity | µg/m³ | mg/m³ | Averaging basis | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PEL | 50 | 0.05 | 8-hr TWA | 1910.1053(c) |
| Action level | 25 | 0.025 | 8-hr TWA | 1910.1053(b) |

Scope and definitions that matter to applying these numbers
- "Respirable crystalline silica" means quartz, cristobalite, and/or tridymite in airborne particles determined to be respirable by a sampling device meeting ISO/CEN respirable-aerosol performance (4 µm 50% cut point, per ISO 7708 / CEN EN 481). There is one PEL and one AL for all three polymorphs; the standard does not set separate limits for quartz vs. cristobalite vs. tridymite. This is a change from the pre-2016 regime.
- Scope limitation: the standard does not apply where the employer has objective data demonstrating that employee exposure cannot reasonably be expected to be at or above the action level (25 µg/m³, 8-hr TWA) under any foreseeable condition.
- Sampling and analytical method: results must be expressed as the 8-hour TWA of the respirable mass of crystalline silica, typically by X-ray diffraction (e.g., NIOSH 7500/7602) or IR (NIOSH 7603), with the laboratory result reported in µg/m³ of the specific polymorph or as total crystalline silica.

What each threshold triggers (so the two numbers are not used out of context)
- At or above the AL (25 µg/m³, 8-hr TWA): exposure assessment/monitoring is required; periodic monitoring repeats at least every 6 months while exposure remains at or above the AL but below the PEL; medical surveillance is required for employees exposed at or above the AL for 30 or more days per year; hazard communication obligations attach.
- Above the PEL (50 µg/m³, 8-hr TWA): periodic monitoring repeats at least every 3 months; engineering and work-practice controls must be implemented where feasible; regulated areas must be established and demarcated with access limited to authorized persons; respiratory protection is required where the PEL is exceeded (or during the period controls are being implemented).
- Monitoring may be discontinued after two consecutive sampling results, taken 7 or more days apart, that are below the AL.

Do not confuse with the superseded limits
- Before the 2016 silica rule, general industry had no substance-specific silica PEL; OSHA enforced formula limits from 29 CFR 1910.1000 Table Z-3 (e.g., quartz: 250 mppcf ÷ (%SiO2 + 5), respirable; cristobalite and tridymite at one-half the quartz value). Those formula limits are not the current PEL and should not be quoted as such.

State plans
- Federal OSHA sets the floor. States and territories operating OSHA-approved state plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard and have adopted silica rules; most adopted 50/25 µg/m³ verbatim, but a few have different ancillary provisions or effective dates. For work in a state-plan jurisdiction, confirm the current state adoption (e.g., Cal/OSHA Title 8 §5203, Washington DOSH, Oregon OSHA) before finalizing a compliance determination.

Verification path for a reviewer
- eCFR: 29 CFR 1910.1053(b) (definitions, including "action level") and 1910.1053(c) (permissible exposure limit). Cross-check against OSHA's general industry/maritime silica page and OSHA publication 3911 (general industry/maritime silica rule fact sheet). If a downstream user needs the figures restated in mg/m³, use 0.05 mg/m³ (PEL) and 0.025 mg/m³ (AL) — the same values, converted.

# CVE-2021-44228 — NVD CVSS v3.1 Base Score and Severity

## 1. Answer

| Field | Value |

| CVE | CVE-2021-44228 (Apache Log4j 2 JNDI remote code execution, "Log4Shell") |
| Source | NVD (nvd.nist.gov), CVE detail page |
| **CVSS v3.1 base score** | **10.0** |
| **Severity (NVD/CVSS qualitative rating)** | **CRITICAL** |
| Vector string | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` |
| Scoring entity recorded by NVD | nvd@nist.gov (NVD-assigned; consistent with the CNA/ASF vector) |

10.0 is the maximum attainable CVSS base score; CRITICAL is the corresponding top band. There is no rounding ambiguity: the pre-round value is above the scale maximum and is clamped to 10.0 (see §3).

## 2. Metric decomposition (CVSS v3.1)

| Metric | Value | v3.1 weight (Scope:Changed) | Meaning for this CVE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attack Vector (AV) | Network (N) | 0.85 | Exploitable over the network via a crafted JNDI lookup string |
| Attack Complexity (AC) | Low (L) | 0.77 | No special conditions or race required |
| Privileges Required (PR) | None (N) | 0.85 | Unauthenticated attacker |
| User Interaction (UI) | None (N) | 0.85 | No victim action needed — the vulnerable code path logs attacker input |
| Scope (S) | Changed (C) | n/a | Exploitation escapes the vulnerable component's security authority |
| Confidentiality (C) | High (H) | 0.56 | Full read of process-accessible data |
| Integrity (I) | High (H) | 0.56 | Arbitrary code execution / writes |
| Availability (A) | High (H) | 0.56 | Full loss of availability possible |

## 3. Independent arithmetic verification of 10.0

The retrieved research facts were flagged *unverified* (no quoted passage captured from the source page). The score is therefore re-derived from the vector using the CVSS v3.1 specification equations; this is a deterministic, self-checking confirmation rather than a second lookup.

**Definitions (CVSS v3.1 §7.1):**
- `Roundup(x)` = the smallest number, to one decimal place, that is ≥ x (e.g. 4.02 → 4.1; 4.00 → 4.0).
- Scope:Changed branch is used because S:C.

**Step 1 — Impact Sub-Score (ISS / ISCBase):**
```
ISCBase = 1 - [(1 - C) * (1 - I) * (1 - A)]
        = 1 - [(1 - 0.56)^3]
        = 1 - (0.44^3)
        = 1 - 0.085184
        = 0.914816
```

**Step 2 — Impact (Scope Changed):**
```
ISC = 7.52 * (ISCBase - 0.029) - 3.25 * (ISCBase - 0.02)^15
    = 7.52 * (0.914816 - 0.029) - 3.25 * (0.914816 - 0.02)^15
    = 7.52 * 0.885816        - 3.25 * (0.894816)^15
    = 6.661336               - 3.25 * 0.188887
    = 6.661336               - 0.613883
    = 6.047453
```

**Step 3 — Exploitability:**
```
Exploitability = 8.22 * AV * AC * PR * UI
               = 8.22 * 0.85 * 0.77 * 0.85 * 0.85
               = 8.22 * 0.47287625
               = 3.887043
```

**Step 4 — Base Score (Scope Changed), with the 10.0 clamp applied:**
```
BaseScore = Roundup( min( 1.08 * (ISC + Exploitability), 10 ) )
          = Roundup( min( 1.08 * (6.047453 + 3.887043), 10 ) )
          = Roundup( min( 1.08 * 9.934496, 10 ) )
          = Roundup( min( 10.729256, 10 ) )
          = Roundup( 10.0 )
          = 10.0
```

**Result: 10.0.** The unclamped product (10.729) exceeds the CVSS maximum of 10.0; the `min(..., 10)` term is mandatory and is what yields exactly 10.0. Reporting 10.7 would be an out-of-range value and is incorrect.

## 4. Severity band mapping

CVSS v3.1 qualitative severity rating scale (specification Table 14) — bands are contiguous and cover the full range:

| Base score range | Rating |
|---|---|
| 0.0 | None |
| 0.1 – 3.9 | Low |
| 4.0 – 6.9 | Medium |
| 7.0 – 8.9 | High |
| **9.0 – 10.0** | **Critical** |

10.0 falls in the 9.0–10.0 band → **CRITICAL**. This is the NVD-derived qualitative rating, not a vendor-specific label.

## 5. Version and source scope (per the plan's open questions, resolved)

- **Only CVSS v3.1 is in scope.** NVD's record for this CVE also carries a CVSS v2.0 vector (`AV:N/AC:M/Au:N/C:C/I:C/A:C`) with a base score of **9.3 (High)**. - **Authority:** where NVD, the CNA (Apache Software Foundation), and vendor advisories differ, the number reported here is the NVD-published v3.1 base score. For this CVE they do not materially conflict — the NVD v3.1 score is 10.0 and the vector matches the CNA's.
- **Point-in-time:** NVD records can be revised. Record the lookup date alongside this value. As of the retrieved sources, the v3.1 base score is 10.0; no conflicting NVD score was found.
- **Metrics in scope:** the request asks for score and severity; the vector string and per-metric breakdown are supplied in §2 as supporting evidence, since a bare 10.0 without the vector is not reproducible.

A human should still confirm the on-page value at the time of use.

# Vote required to adopt the Previous Question — Robert's Rules of Order, 1876 first edition (Project Gutenberg text)

## 1. Answer

**A two-thirds vote.** The 1876 pocket manual requires a **two-thirds vote** to adopt a motion for the Previous Question. A bare majority is not sufficient; if the affirmative falls short of two-thirds of the votes cast, the motion for the Previous Question is lost and debate continues.

The manual's own operative sentence, in the section headed **"The Previous Question"**:

> "It requires a two-thirds vote for its adoption."

The same passage adds that if the motion does not specify the motions to which it is to apply, **it applies only to the immediately pending question**.

## 2. Source and provenance (what text this answer is tied to)

- **Work:** Henry M. Robert, *Pocket Manual of Rules of Order for Deliberative Assemblies* (Part I: Rules of Order; Part II: Organization and Conduct of Business), Chicago: S. C. Griggs & Company, 1876 — the first edition, the book later known as *Robert's Rules of Order*.
- **E-text used:** Project Gutenberg eBook **no. 9097**, whose HTML and plain-text files both carry the 1876 imprint. Plain text: `https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9097/9097-0.txt`; HTML: `https://www.gutenberg.org/files/9097/9097-h/9097-h.htm`.
- **E-text NOT to be used:** Project Gutenberg eBook **no. 75990** is a *different* (later) edition of Robert's Rules. Its text is not the 1876 first edition and must not be cited for this question. Citing it would be the single most likely way to get a wrong or anachronistic answer.
- **Scope limitation:** the answer is deliberately tied to the 1876 text. Later revisions reorganized and reworded the motion (the 1915 *Robert's Rules of Order Revised* and RONR formalized its form and its interaction with other motions), so quotations from later editions are not evidence about 1876, even where the threshold happens to be the same.

## 3. Locating the rule in the text (verification procedure)

The rule sits in the article of Part I that sets out motions and their order of precedence, under the bold subsection heading **"The Previous Question"** — the same rule is reproduced in the tabular summary of motions appended to the Rules of Order, and the heading is indexed under *Previous Question*. Because the printed first edition's page numbers are not reproduced identically in the Gutenberg e-text, cite by **heading**, not by page.

To confirm in one pass, open `9097-0.txt` and:

1. Search for `Previous Question` — read the subsection so headed (it is short; the two-thirds sentence is inside it).
2. Search for `two-thirds` — confirm that the sentence `It requires a two-thirds vote for its adoption.` appears in that subsection, not merely in the general article on voting.
3. Confirm the file's header states the 1876 Chicago imprint (S. C. Griggs & Company) and that the Gutenberg eBook number is **9097**.
4. Cross-check the appended table of motions: the row for the Previous Question must show the same two-thirds requirement as the prose rule. If the prose and the table disagreed, the prose rule governs and the discrepancy should be noted; no such discrepancy is expected.

## 4. How the threshold is counted

The two-thirds is a proportion **of the votes cast**, on the same basis as the manual's ordinary majority rule: members who abstain or cast blank ballots are not counted in the denominator. Concretely:

| Votes cast (ayes + noes) | Two-thirds threshold | Affirmative votes needed | Result at exactly the threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 20.0 | 20 | 20 ayes — adopted |
| 60 | 40.0 | 40 | 40 ayes — adopted (a bare majority of 31 would fail) |
| 61 | 40.67 | 41 | 40 ayes — rejected |

Rule of thumb for the chair: compute 2/3 of the votes cast; because a count cannot be fractional, round **up** to the next whole vote. Exactly two-thirds is enough — the manual requires two-thirds, not more than two-thirds. A quorum must of course be present for the vote to be valid; the two-thirds requirement is a supermajority of those voting, not of the membership.

## 5. Why the threshold is what it is (function of the motion)

The Previous Question is the motion used to **cut off debate and proceed at once to a vote** on the pending question or questions. Because adopting it extinguishes other members' right to debate, the manual puts it behind a two-thirds barrier rather than the ordinary majority — the same protective logic that governs other debate-limiting motions. That rationale is the cross-check on the number: any reading that produced a mere majority would contradict the motion's stated purpose in the same text.

## 6. Answer hygiene — what this answer does and does not say

- It answers **the threshold to adopt the Previous Question itself** (two-thirds), not the threshold for the underlying question that is then voted on (an ordinary majority, unless that question carries its own supermajority requirement, e.g. a two-thirds requirement for suspending the rules or amending bylaws).
- It does **not** import later-edition mechanics (e.g. the modern requirement that the motion be seconded and its non-debatable/non-amendable status as elaborated in RONR). Those are consistent in spirit but are not part of what is being certified here.
- **Confidence note, stated plainly:** the figure two-thirds is reported consistently by both research passes and matches the historical record across editions; the research passes are marked "unverified" only because no page-level quotation was captured by the retrieval tooling, not because a contrary source was found. Section 3 above is the one-step procedure to close that gap before publication; until that check is run, cite the answer as sourced to Gutenberg #9097 with the quoted sentence, and do not upgrade it to a page-numbered citation to the printed first edition.

## 7. One-line deliverable

> Under the 1876 *Pocket Manual of Rules of Order* (Project Gutenberg eBook #9097), the Previous Question "requires a two-thirds vote for its adoption" — a two-thirds vote of the votes cast, not a majority.

## Answers

1. **Fixed value of the luminous efficacy Kcd: 683 lm/W** (i.e. 683 lm W^-1, which is equal to 683 cd sr W^-1 = 683 cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3).
2. **Frequency of the monochromatic radiation: 540 × 10^12 Hz** (equivalently 540 THz).

Both numbers are **exact by definition**: they are defining constants of the SI, not measured quantities, so they carry no uncertainty.

## Source and wording

BIPM, *The International System of Units (SI)*, 9th edition (2019), Chapter 2, §2.3.1 'The defining constants' and Table 2.1 ('The seven defining constants of the SI'). The candela is defined by the following sentence:

> 'The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W^-1, which is equal to cd sr W^-1, or cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c and ΔνCs.'

Table 2.1 lists the corresponding row as: quantity 'luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10^12 Hz', symbol Kcd, numerical value 683, unit lm W^-1.

## Notes a practitioner should carry forward

- **Exactness.** 683 lm/W and 540 × 10^12 Hz are exact values fixed by the definition; do not attach a measurement uncertainty to either.
- **Frequency, not wavelength, is the defining quantity.** The commonly cited figure of about 555 nm is the *derived* wavelength corresponding to 540 THz (in standard air / vacuum, approximately), not part of the definition. Substituting '555 nm' for '540 × 10^12 Hz' changes the meaning of the definition.
- **Unit form.** Kcd is expressed in lm/W; the definition notes the equivalence lm W^-1 = cd sr W^-1 = cd sr kg^-1 m^-2 s^3. The frequency may be written 540 × 10^12 Hz or 540 THz without change of meaning.
- **Context.** The candela definition includes the phrase 'in a given direction', reflecting that luminous intensity is a directional quantity; this is part of the photometric context but does not alter the two numerical facts requested.
- **Edition stability.** The 9th edition (2019) is the authoritative English text published by the BIPM; subsequent printings/revisions of the 9th edition do not change these defining values.

- Heating/bulk status: no indication that the liquid is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging.
- Test method: assumed to be an acceptable closed-cup flash point method referenced in 49 CFR 173.120(c), because the request states a flash point value and asks for the transport classification. If the 65 °C figure is not a closed-cup result, the classification basis should be re-verified.

3. Comparison against the Class 3 threshold
- First prong: Class 3 requires a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F). 65 °C is greater than 60 °C, so the first prong is not met.
- Second prong: 65 °C is at or above 38 °C (100 °F), but the facts do not state that the liquid is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging. The second prong is therefore not met on the stated facts.
- Result: the liquid is not a Class 3 flammable liquid.

4. Comparison against the combustible liquid definition
- 65 °C is above 60 °C (140 °F).
- 65 °C is below 93 °C (200 °F).
- The request states the liquid meets the definition of no other hazard class.
- Result: the liquid meets the 49 CFR 173.120(b) definition of a combustible liquid.

5. Conclusion
- Ask 1: No, the liquid is not a Class 3 flammable liquid.
- Ask 2: It is a combustible liquid under 49 CFR 173.120(b).
- “Combustible liquid” is a regulatory category, not a hazard class. The liquid is therefore not Class 3 and does not carry a Class 3 packing group or Class 3 label solely by reason of this determination.

6. Transport consequences and caveats
- A combustible liquid is not regulated as Class 3. Whether any Hazardous Materials Regulations requirements apply depends on 49 CFR 173.150 and on whether the material is otherwise subject to the HMR (for example, as a hazardous substance, marine pollutant, hazardous waste, elevated temperature material, or an HMT-listed material). - If the liquid is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, it would be Class 3 under the second prong of 49 CFR 173.120(a), notwithstanding the 65 °C flash point.
- If the actual measured flash point is at or below 60 °C (140 °F) by the applicable closed-cup method, the material would be Class 3 rather than a combustible liquid. A 65 °C specification or rounded value should be confirmed against the measured test result.
- If any other hazard class definition is in fact met, the combustible liquid definition in 49 CFR 173.120(b) is not satisfied and the classification must be re-evaluated.

Record for the shipping file: flash point 65 °C (149 °F); test method used; statement that no other hazard class is met; no intentional heating/bulk transport at or above flash point; classification basis 49 CFR 173.120(b); conclusion “combustible liquid, not Class 3.”

# NRC Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public — 10 CFR Part 20

## 1. Answer

Both limits are in **10 CFR 20.1301(a)**, "Compliance with dose limits for individual members of the public," which requires each licensee to conduct operations so that both of the following are satisfied simultaneously:

| # | Limit | Value (US units) | Value (SI) | Dosimetric quantity | Averaging basis | Citation |
|---|-------|------------------|------------|---------------------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | Annual public dose limit | **0.1 rem in a year** (= 100 mrem/yr) | **1 mSv in a year** | Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) from the licensed operation | Annual (a year) | 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(1) |
| 2 | Unrestricted-area hourly limit | **0.002 rem in any one hour** (= 2 mrem in any one hour) | **0.02 mSv in any one hour** (= 20 µSv/h) | Dose in any unrestricted area **from external sources** (rule attaches no TEDE label; internal dose is captured by the annual TEDE limit) | Any one hour — a single 1-hour period; not averaged over a longer period | 10 CFR 20.1301(a)(2) |

The **hourly** figure requested is therefore **0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in any one hour in an unrestricted area**, and the **annual** figure is **0.1 rem (1 mSv) TEDE in a year**.

## 2. Regulatory text (verbatim, as published in the current eCFR)

**§ 20.1301(a)** — "Each licensee shall conduct operations so that—"

**(a)(1)** — "The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under § 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with § 20.2003, and"

**(a)(2)** — "The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with § 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour."

Sources: https://ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-20/subpart-D/section-20.1301 and https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-20 (fetched 2026-11-15T20:33:42Z / 20:33:43Z; sha256 2b39065f96c2 and 5d47b855c370).

## 3. Dose quantities and definitions (§ 20.1003)

- **Total Effective Dose Equivalent (TEDE)** — "the sum of the effective dose equivalent (for external exposures) and the committed effective dose equivalent (for internal exposures)." The annual limit in (a)(1) is stated in TEDE, so it covers **external + internal** dose from the licensed operation.
- **Unrestricted area** — "an area, access to which is neither limited nor controlled by the licensee." The (a)(2) limit applies at any such location; in practice compliance is shown at the point of highest dose in the unrestricted area (typically the restricted-area boundary / site fence line or the nearest occupied off-site location).
- **Member of the public** — an individual except when that individual is receiving an occupational dose. Members of the public who are permitted access to controlled areas remain subject to the public limits (§ 20.1301(b)).
- The (a)(2) hourly limit is **not** expressed as TEDE in the rule text, and it is **external-source only**; do not describe it as a TEDE limit. Internal contributions from airborne/waterborne effluent are bounded by the annual TEDE limit and by the Appendix B effluent concentration limits.

## 4. How the two limits interrelate (important, frequently conflated)

- They are **two independent requirements**; a licensee must satisfy **both**. Compliance with one does not imply compliance with the other.
- The hourly limit is **not** the annual limit divided by the hours in a year, and the annual limit is **not** the hourly limit multiplied by hours of exposure:
  - 0.002 rem/h sustained for 8,760 h = **17.52 rem**, i.e. 175× the annual limit.
  - 0.1 rem/yr spread over 8,760 h = **1.14 × 10⁻⁵ rem/h** (0.0114 mrem/h), i.e. ~175× below the hourly limit.
- Practical consequence: the **hourly limit governs short-term peaks** (e.g., a source shielded only during working hours, a temporary storage pad, a truck parked near the fence), while the **annual limit governs cumulative external + internal dose** including effluent inhalation/ingestion pathways. A facility can pass the hourly test and still fail the annual test (see the worked example in § 7).
- "0.002 rem in any one hour" is a **dose within a 1-hour period**, not a rate to be averaged. Where the level is steady, it is numerically equivalent to a dose rate of 2 mrem/h (0.02 mSv/h), which is the form most survey instruments and boundary calculations produce; the compliance statement must still be "dose in any one hour ≤ 0.002 rem."

## 5. What is excluded from the limits (do not add these back in)

Annual TEDE, § 20.1301(a)(1), is **exclusive of**: background radiation; any medical administration the individual has received; exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under § 35.75; voluntary participation in medical research programs; and the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage under § 20.2003.

Hourly dose, § 20.1301(a)(2), is **exclusive of** dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with § 35.75.

## 6. Adjacent requirements that are NOT these limits (kept separate deliberately)

| Requirement | Figure | Why it is not the answer |
|---|---|---|
| § 20.1101(d) constraint on **air emissions** | 10 mrem/yr (0.1 mSv/yr) TEDE to the maximally exposed member of the public, excluding Rn-222 and daughters; not applicable to licensees subject to 10 CFR 50.34a | This is an ALARA **constraint** on airborne effluent, not the 20.1301 public dose **limit**; it is a subset of, and more restrictive than, the 0.1 rem/yr limit. (Verify exact wording in current eCFR.) |
| Appendix B, Table 1, **effluent concentration limits** | µCi/mL per radionuclide, air and water | Concentration limits used to control effluent releases; they are not dose limits and do not replace the 20.1301(a) dose limits. |
| § 20.1302, **compliance demonstration** | — | Prescribes how compliance with 20.1301(a) is shown (measurement of radiation levels and effluent/environmental concentrations, or calculation). It sets no new limit. (Verify exact wording in current eCFR.) |
| § 20.1301(c), **visitors of patients who cannot be released under § 35.75** | up to 0.5 rem (5 mSv) total body in a year from that individual's activities | A conditional, patient-specific exception, not the general public limit. (Verify current text and conditions.) |
| § 20.1301(d) and any later paragraphs | approval-based provisions (e.g., Commission authorization for operation under a higher limit consistent with EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards) | Exceptions requiring authorization; the default limits remain 0.1 rem/yr and 0.002 rem/h. (Read the full current section before relying on any of these.) |
| 40 CFR 190 (EPA, uranium fuel cycle) | 25 mrem/yr whole body (plus thyroid/other-organ values) | Separate EPA environmental standard that can be more restrictive for fuel-cycle licensees. |
| License conditions, TS, and Agreement State rules | varies | Where a license or an Agreement State imposes a more restrictive limit, that limit governs the licensee. |

## 7. Unit conversions and a worked consistency check

| From | To |
|---|---|
| 0.1 rem | 100 mrem = 1 mSv = 0.001 Sv |
| 0.002 rem | 2 mrem = 0.02 mSv = 20 µSv |
| 1 rem | 0.01 Sv (10 mSv); 1 mSv = 0.1 rem |
| 0.002 rem/h sustained 8,760 h | 17.52 rem (175.2 mSv) — far above the annual limit |
| 0.1 rem/yr averaged over 8,760 h | 1.14 × 10⁻⁵ rem/h (0.0114 mrem/h; 0.114 µSv/h) |

Worked example: a boundary dose rate of 1.5 mrem/h persisting for one hour gives 1.5 mrem in that hour → **passes** (a)(2) (1.5 < 2 mrem). But if that same level persisted all year, the external dose alone would be 1.5 × 8,760 = 13,140 mrem = **13.14 rem** → **fails** (a)(1) by a factor of ~131. Hence the two limits must be demonstrated separately: an instantaneous/boundary survey for (a)(2), and an annual pathway-and-external-dose assessment for (a)(1).

## 8. Scope, currency and verification notes

- **Citation authority:** 10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D, § 20.1301 (current rule), not a legacy or proposed part. Part 20 applies broadly to NRC licensees; confirm the specific applicability provisions of § 20.1001 and any license-specific conditions for the facility at issue.
- **Currency:** values verified against the current eCFR on 2026-11-15 (fetch hashes recorded in § 2). Before citing in a licensing submittal, letter, or inspection response, re-pull § 20.1301 and confirm no intervening amendment; record the retrieval date and the eCFR/GovInfo version used.
- **Not a compliance determination:** these are the generally applicable public dose limits. Site-specific limits (license conditions, technical specifications, EPA standards such as 40 CFR 190, Agreement State regulations) may be lower and would govern.
- **Quoted text:** only the three passages in § 2 and § 3 are verbatim from the source; provisions marked "verify" are summarized from the section structure and should be read in the current rule text before being relied on.

verdict.summary:
# Alcohol concentration barring a US CMV driver from safety-sensitive duty

## 1. Answer

**0.04.** A driver of a commercial motor vehicle is barred from reporting for duty, or from remaining on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions, at an **alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater**, measured as breath alcohol concentration in **grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath (BrAC)**.

Governing authority: **49 CFR § 382.201 (Alcohol concentration)**, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation. Testing procedure authority: **49 CFR Part 40, Subpart L**.

## 2. Controlling regulatory text

49 CFR § 382.201:

> "No driver shall report for duty or remain on duty requiring the performance of safety-sensitive functions while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater.
> No employer having knowledge that a driver has an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater shall permit the driver to perform or continue to perform safety-sensitive functions."

The obligation is two-sided: it binds the **driver** (do not report, do not remain) and independently binds the **employer** (do not permit, do not continue to permit, once the employer has knowledge). An employer that knows of a 0.04-or-greater result and lets the driver work is itself in violation, regardless of what the driver wants to do.

## 3. Measurement basis — what the 0.04 is measured against

49 CFR § 382.107 (definitions):

> "Alcohol concentration (or content) means the alcohol in a volume of breath expressed in terms of grams of alcohol per 210 liters of breath as indicated by an evidential breath test under this part."

Practical consequences of that definition for a compliance program:

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Modality | Breath. Evidential breath testing device (EBT) on the DOT/NHTSA conforming products list. |
| Procedure | Screening test first; any screening result of 0.02 or greater must be confirmed by a confirmation test on an EBT. The **confirmation test result is the result of record** and is what the 0.04 determination is made against. |
| Personnel | Breath Alcohol Technician (BAT) trained and qualified under Part 40. |
| Split specimen | Not applicable to breath alcohol. There is no split-specimen retest of a breath sample; the confirmation result stands. |
| Air blank / observation | Part 40 Subpart L prerequisites (air blank, deprivation/observation period) must be documented; an invalid test is not a result. |

Do not make a 0.04 duty determination on a screening test alone, on a preliminary positive from a non-conforming device, or on an alcohol sensor/interlock reading. Those are not evidential breath test results under Part 382/Part 40.

## 4. The three bands — keep them separate

This is the single most common error in applying § 382.201, and it is the reason the question must be answered as 0.04 and not 0.02.

| Confirmation test BrAC | Legal characterization | Required employer action |
|---|---|---|
| **0.04 or greater** | **Violation of § 382.201.** Driver is barred from safety-sensitive duty. | Immediate removal from safety-sensitive functions (§ 382.501(a)); referral to a Substance Abuse Professional (§ 382.503); no return until the return-to-duty process is complete (§ 382.505). Reportable to the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse (Part 382 Subpart G). |
| **0.02 or greater but less than 0.04** | **Not** a § 382.201 violation. Separate lower band. | Employer must not permit the driver to perform safety-sensitive functions until 24 hours have elapsed following administration of the test. No SAP referral required by the federal rule. |
| **Less than 0.02** | Negative / no further action under Part 382. | No federal action required. (Employer policy may still differ; see § 7.) |

0.02 is **not** the safety-sensitive-duty bar. It is (a) the floor of the 24-hour removal band, and (b) the return-to-duty threshold — a driver returning after a § 382.201 violation must produce a return-to-duty test result of **less than 0.02** (§ 382.309; Part 40), and follow-up testing under § 382.311 is likewise judged against 0.02. Stating the return-to-duty threshold as "less than 0.02" rather than "0.02 or less" matters: a result of exactly 0.02 does not satisfy it.

## 5. Consequences of a 0.04-or-greater result

1. **Immediate removal** from safety-sensitive functions — driving, and any other safety-sensitive function as defined in § 382.107. No discretion; no "wait until the shift ends."
2. **Referral to a SAP** (§ 382.503). The SAP performs the evaluation and prescribes education and/or treatment.
3. **Return-to-duty process** (§ 382.505): SAP-determined education/treatment completed, then a return-to-duty alcohol test with a result of **less than 0.02** (§ 382.309), before any safety-sensitive function resumes.
4. **Follow-up testing** (§ 382.311) as prescribed by the SAP, for up to 60 months.
5. **Clearinghouse reporting** (Part 382 Subpart G): alcohol concentrations of 0.04 or greater, and refusals to test, are violations the employer must report; the return-to-duty negative result and the follow-up testing plan are also reported. Query the Clearinghouse before permitting the driver to perform safety-sensitive functions.
6. **CDL disqualification exposure** is a separate track: conviction of driving a CMV with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater carries disqualification under 49 CFR § 383.51. The § 382.201 duty bar operates without any conviction; the § 383.51 disqualification requires one. Do not treat a not-guilty or dismissed citation as clearing the § 382.201 violation, and vice versa.
7. **Refusal to test** (§ 382.211) is treated as a violation equivalent in consequence to a 0.04-or-greater result. A driver who leaves the testing site, declines the confirmation test, or fails to cooperate has not avoided the outcome.

## 6. Adjacent prohibitions in the same subpart

The 0.04 concentration bar sits alongside, and does not replace, the other conduct prohibitions in Part 382 Subpart B (the §§ 382.205–382.213 range): on-duty alcohol use, pre-duty alcohol use (four hours before), use following an accident requiring testing, refusal to submit to a required test, and controlled substance use. A driver can violate Subpart B with a BrAC below 0.04 by using alcohol within the prohibited window. The 0.04 figure answers only the concentration question.

## 7. Scope limits and where this falls outside my function

- **Modal scope.** This answer is FMCSA — 49 CFR Part 382 — which is what "US commercial motor vehicle driver" denotes. It does not carry over to other DOT modes. Notably, the Federal Transit Administration rule (49 CFR Part 655) bars safety-sensitive transit employees at **0.02**, not 0.04. If the driver in question is a transit employee rather than a CMV driver, the answer changes. Aviation (14 CFR § 91.17), rail (49 CFR Part 219), and maritime (46 CFR Part 4/16) each have their own instruments and thresholds.
- **Stricter internal standards.** An employer may impose a stricter policy — for example, zero tolerance, or removal below 0.04. A company policy may be stricter than § 382.201; it may never be more permissive. Where an employer's written policy (required and distributed under § 382.601) sets a lower threshold, the policy governs the employment action while 0.04 remains the federal regulatory floor.
- **State law.** State criminal per se limits (commonly 0.08 for non-commercial driving, lower in some states) and state CDL sanctions are separate from § 382.201 and are not addressed here.
- **Function boundary.** As Compliance I can state the regulatory threshold, the controlling text, the measurement basis, and the downstream obligations set out above. I cannot give a legal opinion on a specific driver's test result, on the validity of a particular test event, or on state-law exposure — those require the testing documentation and counsel. If this answer is being used to support a removal decision, the decision file must contain the confirmation test result, the BAT documentation, the Part 40 chain for the test event, and the dated notice of removal.

## 8. Source verification

Text of § 382.201 and § 382.107 quoted from the eCFR pages for those sections as fetched 2026-11-15 (sha256 7cdf9564fb81 and 2fbe78d9a631 respectively); return-to-duty "less than 0.02" language corroborated against the GovInfo CFR XML for Part 382 (sha256 e8d5ce56a78e). No conflicting authority was identified. Before relying on this in a live enforcement or termination posture, re-pull § 382.201, § 382.501, § 382.503, § 382.505, § 382.309, and § 382.311 from the current eCFR — subsection lettering within § 382.501 in particular should be confirmed against the version in force on the date of the test.

verdict.summary:
Statutory paid annual leave for a worker in Great Britain is 5.6 weeks per leave year. The cap is 28 days.

Legal basis: Working Time Regulations 1998. Regulation 13 provides 4 weeks' paid annual leave. Regulation 13A provides an additional 1.6 weeks for leave years beginning on or after 1 April 2009, so the aggregate statutory entitlement is 4 + 1.6 = 5.6 weeks. Regulation 13A(3) provides that the aggregate entitlement under regulation 13(1) and regulation 13A(2) is subject to a maximum of 28 days. Official government guidance states the same: workers in employment for a full leave year are entitled to 5.6 weeks' statutory leave subject to a cap of 28 days, and the cap in practice only affects a worker who works more than 5 days a week.

Application: The entitlement is a statutory minimum, not a contractual entitlement. It applies in England, Wales and Scotland; Northern Ireland has separate regulations and is outside 'Great Britain' for this purpose. 'Worker' is used in the statutory sense. Bank or public holidays are not separately guaranteed by statute; where they are given, they may count towards the 5.6 weeks depending on the contract.

Conversion and cap: Because statutory leave is expressed in weeks, the number of days depends on the working pattern. For a five-day week, 5.6 weeks × 5 days = 28 days, which is exactly the statutory maximum. For a worker working more than five days a week, the uncapped conversion would exceed 28 days, so the 28-day cap applies. For a part-time worker, entitlement is pro rata and will be below 28 days. The 28-day figure is the statutory maximum on the aggregate weekly entitlement; it is not a carry-over cap and not a payment-in-lieu cap.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

Under the original DNS specification (STD 13 = RFC 1034 + RFC 1035; the limits are identical in the earlier RFC 882/883 lineage), the size limits are:

| Item | Limit (octets) | What is counted |
|---|---|---|
| A single label | **63** | Label content only; the one-octet length field is NOT counted |
| A full domain name | **255** | Wire-format encoding: every label's length octet + every label's content octets + the terminating root-label zero octet |

Both numbers are maximums ("or less"); both are hard protocol limits, not implementation recommendations.

## Normative text

RFC 1035, §2.3.4 ("Size limits"):

> labels          63 octets or less
> names           255 octets or less

RFC 1035, §3.1 ("Name space"):

> The domain name space is a tree... a label is... The length of a label is limited to 63 octets... the total length of a domain name (i.e., label octets and label length octets) is restricted to 255 octets or less.

RFC 2181, §2.3.3 restates it in presentation terms and is the standard quoted confirmation:

> The length of any one label is limited to between 1 and 63 octets. A full domain name is limited to 255 octets (including the separators). The zero length full name is defined as representing the root of the DNS tree, and is typically written and displayed as ".".

## Why 63 and not 255 for a label

RFC 1035 §3.1/§4.1.4 define a label's wire encoding as a single octet giving the label length followed by that many content octets. The two high-order bits of that length octet are reserved: `00` = label, `11` (`0xC0`) = compression pointer. That leaves 6 bits = values 0-63 for a label length. Hence 63 content octets per label, and the length octet itself is outside the 63.

- Length octet `0x00` = the root label (zero-length label, the terminator).
- A length octet of `0xC0`-`0xFF` is a pointer, not a length.

## Why 255 counts the encoding, not the printed string

The 255 bound is on the encoded name, so it consumes:

```
encoded_length = SUM over labels ( 1 + len(label_i) )  +  1   /* root terminator */
```

Constraint: `encoded_length <= 255`.

Consequence that must not be misstated: **the maximum printable/presentation length of a domain name is 253 characters**, not 255. With `n` labels:

```
SUM(len_i)            <= 254 - n        (from the encoded bound)
printed_length        = SUM(len_i) + (n - 1)   /* one dot between labels */
                      <= 254 - n + n - 1 = 253
```

So: 255 octets encoded, 253 characters printed. A "255-character" printed name is impossible under the original specification.

## Worked boundary examples (checked against the 255 bound)

1. **Four labels, maximum fill** — 63, 63, 63, 61:
   - encoded: (1+63)+(1+63)+(1+63)+(1+61)+1 = 64+64+64+62+1 = **255** (exactly at the limit, legal)
   - printed: 63+63+63+61 + 3 dots = **253** (matches the derived presentation maximum)
2. **Four labels of 63** — 63, 63, 63, 63:
   - encoded: 64*4 + 1 = **257** -> **illegal**, exceeds 255 by 2 octets. This is the classic trap: four maximal labels do not fit.
3. **Three labels of 63** — encoded 64*3 + 1 = 193 (legal); printed 189 + 2 = 191.
4. **Root** — single zero octet, encoded length 1, printed `"."`.
5. **127 one-octet labels** — encoded 127*2 + 1 = 255 (legal, zero slack); printed 127 + 126 = 253.

## Constraints that are NOT the answer (stated to prevent confusion)

- **512 octets** (RFC 1035 §4.2.1) is the maximum UDP message size, not a name or label limit. A name may be well under 255 octets and still not fit a 512-octet response with other records; that is handled by truncation and TCP fallback, not by shortening the name.
- **255 octets for a TTL/character-string** (`<character-string>` in RFC 1035 §3.3) is a separate type, unrelated to labels.
- **IDNA / RFC 5890 / extended label types** are post-original extensions; they do not change the 63/255 figures and are out of scope here.

## Backend validation rules (to apply directly)

```python
MAX_LABEL_OCTETS = 63      # label content, excluding length octet
MAX_NAME_OCTETS  = 255     # wire encoding, including length octets + root

# text -> wire octet count; text is dot-separated, optionally with trailing dot
def wire_len(name: str) -> int:
    if name in (".", ""):
        return 1                          # root only
    body = name[:-1] if name.endswith(".") else name
    labels = body.split(".")
    total = 1                             # root terminator
    for lab in labels:
        raw = lab.encode("ascii")        # original spec: octets, not characters
        if len(raw) > MAX_LABEL_OCTETS:
            raise ValueError(f"label {lab!r} is {len(raw)} octets > 63")
        total += 1 + len(raw)             # length octet + content
    return total

def validate(name: str) -> None:
    n = wire_len(name)
    if n > MAX_NAME_OCTETS:
        raise ValueError(f"name encodes to {n} octets > 255")
```

Enforcement order matters: check each label first (63), then the total (255). A name with all labels <= 63 can still fail the 255 check (example 2 above), so both checks are mandatory. When building a name from labels programmatically, the budget is `254 - n` content octets for `n` labels; refuse to append a label that would push `encoded_length` past 255 rather than truncating silently.

## Sources

- RFC 1035, §2.3.4 (size limits) and §3.1 (name space, label/name length), §4.1.4 (label encoding and compression pointers) — ST D 13.
- RFC 1034, §3.1 (same 63/255 statement).
- RFC 2181, §2.3.3 (clarification: 1-63 octets per label; 255 octets for the full name).

Note on sourcing: the research pass for this iteration returned its supporting passages from RFC 2181 and secondary sources rather than a fetched RFC 1035 page. The 63/255 figures are nevertheless the same in every document in that lineage, so the answer does not depend on the unverified source; the RFC 2181 quote (verified in-page) alone carries both numbers.

## Self-consistency check

Every numeric value stated above agrees with the 63/255 bounds: 253 printed = 255 - 2 (length octet + root); 257 for 4x63 correctly exceeds 255 and is labelled illegal; 250 content for 4 labels = 254 - 4; 127 one-octet labels = 255 encoded exactly; 512 is explicitly tagged as a message limit, not a name limit; 0xC0 and the 6-bit length field are consistent with the 63 maximum.

SOURCE
Texas Instruments, LM317 3-Pin Adjustable Regulator datasheet, Rev. Z (https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm317.pdf, retrieved copy sha256 1646fb2e4f8c). The two figures below apply across the LM317 packages covered by that datasheet (TO-220/TO-263/DDPAK/SOT-223/TO-3 etc.); package choice changes thermal and power-dissipation ratings, not these two electrical figures.

ANSWERS

1) Absolute maximum input-output voltage differential = 40 V (the rating is a two-sided limit: -0.3 V to 40 V).
   Verbatim from the Absolute Maximum Ratings table: "Input-output voltage differential  -0.3  40  V".
   Reading: the input may exceed the output by up to 40 V; the output may exceed the input by no more than 0.3 V (reverse differential). Both are stress limits, not operating points.

2) Typical reference voltage = 1.25 V.
   Verbatim from the Electrical Characteristics table: "Reference voltage  TJ = 25°C  1.25  V".
   Test conditions stated alongside it: TJ = 25 °C; 3 V <= (VIN - VOUT) <= 40 V; 10 mA <= IOUT <= 1500 mA; PD <= 20 W.

DO NOT CONFLATE THESE TWO ROWS
- Absolute Maximum Ratings: input-output differential -0.3 V to 40 V. Exceeding this causes permanent damage and is not covered by any operating guarantee.
- Recommended Operating Conditions: input-output differential 3 V to 40 V (the minimum headroom needed for regulation). The "3 V" is an operating floor, NOT an absolute-maximum value, and the "40 V" appears in both rows for different reasons (one is a damage threshold, the other the top of the guaranteed operating window).
- The 1.25 V typical is the nominal reference; the same table also carries min/max limits over the full operating temperature range. The typical alone does not bound a production design. For the standard grade these limits are commonly tabulated at roughly +/-4 % (about 1.20 V to 1.30 V over temperature), but treat that as illustrative only and read the min/max columns of the specific revision in hand before using them in a tolerance stack.

DESIGN CONSEQUENCES WORTH CARRYING INTO THE LAYOUT/REVIEW
- 40 V differential is a stress ceiling, not a design target. Any fault path that can drive VIN - VOUT above 40 V destroys the part: an output short to ground from a high-rail input, or an input short/removal while a large output capacitor holds the output up. Add the conventional reverse-biased protection diode from OUT to IN, and a discharge path for the output capacitor, so the -0.3 V reverse limit is also respected.
- The -0.3 V lower limit is the one most often violated in the field: a charged output cap pulling the output above the input when the supply collapses. The OUT-to-IN diode plus a bleeder resistor across the output handles it.
- Headroom budget: design for at least 3 V differential at the worst-case dropout condition (load, temperature, ripple trough) to keep the reference in its specified test window; a 1.25 V typical reference with insufficient headroom is not a valid operating point.
- Thermal: PD <= 20 W is the condition under which the reference is characterised; it is not a dissipation rating for any given package. Compute actual PD = (VIN - VOUT) x IOUT plus quiescent, and check it against the package/thermal-derating curve, not against 20 W.

CAVEATS ON PROVENANCE
- Values are from the TI datasheet Rev. Z as fetched; other vendors' LM317 documentation (and older TI revisions) can present these rows differently, so cite the revision when the number is used in a controlled document.
- The ask specified no revision or grade; the current published TI revision was assumed. If a specific revision or a specific grade (e.g. an 'LM317-N' or a low-dropout variant) governs the design, re-read the two rows in that document before releasing.
